prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

statement.case_for: I keep B022 as my preferred single-part prize with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer. The case is a quantitative prediction (the 2011 continuum model, in which moire interference flattens the bands at a specific angle) followed seven years later by an experiment that found correlated insulators and superconductivity at exactly that angle, then by reproduction in many independent laboratories, including by methods other than transport. What is rewarded is the existence of a new tunable platform for strongly correlated electrons and the model-experiment link, and the citation is worded around those and not around the pairing mechanism. That is the same standard we applied to other correlated-electron discoveries whose mechanism was open when they were honoured. The credit also maps cleanly on to the supplied names: the theory pair and the experimental leader, with no missing prediction of the kind that weakens B054. After round 1 I see nothing that changes my view that this is the strongest new-quantum-behaviour case on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, raised by Johansson, Lindroth and Mehlig, is maturity: the decisive experiment is eight years old, the pairing mechanism and the nature of the correlated insulators are not settled, and twist-angle disorder still limits sample-to-sample reproducibility. B036 is older, more settled and has five explicit supporters, and I accept that as a real argument and not only a count. Credit is incomplete as well: Yuan Cao and the other 2018 first authors cannot be named under the three-person limit, and earlier twisted-graphene band theory could be argued as a precursor. If the committee decides that interpretation must settle before recognition, B036 is the defensible choice and I would not obstruct it.

responses.point: Lindroth keeps B022 only as an alternative because the physics is remarkable but not ready, citing the open pairing mechanism and the twist-angle disorder, and she prefers waiting.
responses.response: The chair asked what would change my view, so I will be concrete. The recognised object is the magic-angle flat band and the correlated and superconducting phases it hosts, not the mechanism, and those have been reproduced by groups using transport, scanning tunnelling spectroscopy and compressibility measurements. Disorder limits how uniform samples are, but it has not made the phases themselves disappear from one laboratory to the next. What would change my mind is evidence that the superconducting state is an artefact of device conditions, or that the flat-band picture fails to account for the spectroscopy, and I know of neither. Waiting for the mechanism could mean waiting a long time; I would not take that stance for a discovery that has been reproduced this widely.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B036 first as a mature, reproduced measurement advance, and in round 1 lists B022 as an alternative while listing the 2005 and 2012 overlap and the priority history as open.
responses.response: I accept the maturity and reproducibility of the 10^-18 result, and this is why B036 is my first alternative. My remaining hesitation is the one you and four colleagues all record: whether a Katori and Ye citation reads as a new regime or as a continuation of the 2005 comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes, and nobody has yet shown that this can be settled in a citation. I cannot verify the priority history against the archives and should say so; Lemonde, Takamoto and Ludlow are outside my field. If the atomic physicists on this committee can write the distinction into a citation and confirm the names, I would be content to join B036. I am not there yet, because I think the flat-band discovery opens more new physics per unit of recognition.

responses.point: Johansson, who ranked B022 eighth at the opening, cites its recent date and unsettled mechanism and says he would not support B054 without a revised credit list.
responses.response: I agree on B054 and I have conceded that the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang cannot be fixed within a three-name list. On B022 I understand why a member with a different field would weigh recency heavily, and I do not claim your concern is unreasonable. My answer is that the phases were found in 2018 and have been confirmed repeatedly since, which makes this a reproduced discovery and not a preliminary result. Your own point about B036 also applies to B022: you moved to B036 after seeing the opening ballots, and you are the member who ranked it seventh and who flags the 2005 and 2012 overlap. If that objection is stronger than you now allow, then B022 is a legitimate comparison and not only a minority view.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B022 with Bistritzer, but calls the maturity objection serious and prefers B036 and B046 as alternatives.
responses.response: We agree on the scientific case and on the three names, and I note that you withdrew your earlier two-name proposal. I treat the maturity objection as a risk the committee can accept, while you treat it as more serious; the difference is small. I would resist your suggestion that a prize should wait only if it concerns the pairing mechanism: that mechanism may take a decade, and the 2018 findings would still be what we are crediting. If you and I are the only two who put B022 first, the honest outcome of the discussion may be that B036 prevails, and I would accept that on the merits and not as an effort to agree with the majority.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept recognising twisted bilayer graphene before the superconducting pairing mechanism is understood.
How to represent Yuan Cao and the other 2018 first authors, and earlier twisted-graphene band theory, under the three-person limit.

Whether lattice clocks can be separated from the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes in a citation, and whether Katori and Ye are exactly the right pair; I cannot check this and rely on colleagues in atomic physics.
I am working from recollection of dates and priorities, which I have not verified against the record.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. I work in theoretical magnetism and electronic structure at Uppsala and have no stated tie to the candidates on B022, B036 or B054. I chaired the committee for the 2025 prize, which does not bear on any shortlisted candidate. I defer on atomic physics and astroparticle physics.
